decision: A tad dataset is DuckDB's EXPORT DATABASE folder - one JSON-lines file per table - edited with SQL and brought back to canonical, diffable files; jq and Miller work on the same files.
why: Everything queryable, versioned and diffable in one place; measured in the spike: a no-op round trip leaves zero diff at 200,000 rows, one changed row is one changed line.
rejected: Doltgres and Dolt (history where a pull request cannot show it); gitsheets (no SQL, no joins); GlueSQL (an engine reinvented, without ALTER TABLE); SQLite with sqlite-diffable.
sources: duckdb-spike, tad-origin-log, duckdb-export, dolt, gitsheets, sqlite-diffable

decision: tad was extracted from a repository that already worked (the software-engineering canon), not designed first in the abstract.
why: An abstraction is right only once it has met a real case; designing first risked assumptions that would not survive real content.

decision: Each repository vendored the engine as a git subrepo at .tad/, pinned in a readable .gitrepo, one commit per sync. Superseded 2026-11-11: copies drifted (three of four older); tad is now called, not copied - released binaries, pinned per repository, moved weekly (2026-11-11-one-release-path, 2026-11-11-pins-moved-by-the-lab).
why: Tested against git subtree on a real update: subrepo writes one commit per sync instead of two and states the pinned commit plainly.
rejected: git subtree (two commits per sync, the pin buried in a commit trailer).

decision: tad is released by release-please (versions and changelog from conventional commits) with the package conveyor building binaries in the same run; the tag-triggered workflow is gone.
why: One release path, no manual version bumps; a tag made with GitHub's own token cannot start another workflow, so the binaries are built in the same run.
rejected: Tagging by hand with land --tag as the release path; keeping both paths.

decision: The lab machine moves each repository's tad pin (bin/update-pins.sh, weekly), landing through land so each repository's CI decides.
why: A pull request opened by a workflow with GitHub's own token starts no CI, so a pure-GitHub updater would open unchecked pull requests; the lab machine already holds a token and lands through checks.
rejected: A GitHub workflow with GitHub's token (its pull requests start no CI); the author's personal token as a secret in four repositories (spreads the key); a GitHub App (the clean CI-native way - needs the author's setup; a later upgrade).

decision: tad in Rust: tables declared as data (after Frictionless Table Schema); one tool - check, canonical form, row edits with a check, documents rendered from data; proven equal to the Python version on all four repositories (same verdicts, same documents) before any switch; delivered by the package conveyor instead of vendored; ocoeco's shapes become a tad declaration. The tool is delivered by the package conveyor (for CI and machines); the library is taken as a Rhizoid cutting where a project builds on it (ocoeco) - as tad's own path already says, a rhizcut in every repository. Corrected 2026-11-12 by 2026-11-12-sql-again: SQL is not optional - tad answers real SQL through an embedded SQLite.
why: The author: tad stays general and Python leaves. The four schemas need no database engine: their 41 tables use only patterns, allowed values, required fields and one list column.
rejected: Rust bindings to DuckDB keeping schema.sql (a database engine to validate text); Dolt (a separate store); keeping the vendored copies.

decision: When the four repositories switch to tad, their documents are re-rendered by today's renderer; the canon's and Rhizoid's change visibly, and that is said in the switch's own change.
why: Their vendored copies are older; the switch is the first time they get today's renderer. A change people did not expect should be announced, not discovered.
rejected: Porting the older renderers too, to switch without visible change.

decision: tad's SQL engine is a port in tad's own words (load the declared tables, run a statement, give the tables back), and its adapter today is DuckDB's pinned standalone binary, checked by fingerprint and installed beside tad; a stand-in serves the tests; an embedded DuckDB stays possible as another adapter if it ever builds statically.
why: Measured (carrying-duckdb): embedding costs six minutes per build, 66 MB, and no static release; the standalone binary is fast, published for both architectures and already trusted by the feeds.
rejected: Embedding DuckDB now (no static build, slow builds, a large binary).

decision: How pages read is declared in tables.toml ([site] and [pages.<table>]) and rendered by tad; no repository keeps a renderer of its own. Refined the same day by 2026-11-12-tad-is-text-as-data: presentation stays declared as data, but in the renderer's own file, not in tables.toml, and the renderer leaves tad.
why: The canon kept its own renderer only for its presentation; declared as data, its seven pages came out identical but for the notice line, and any repository can say how it reads.
rejected: A renderer per repository (code each must keep, and DuckDB with it in the canon's case).

decision: tad answers real SQL again: tad sql runs a statement over the declared tables through an embedded SQLite - a query reads them, a change is checked by tad (every row and rule) before the tables are written back in canonical form, as the Python version did with DuckDB. Proven equal on the four repositories' own queries before anyone relies on it. Superseded the same day by 2026-11-12-sql-is-duckdb: the original 2026-09 research had already weighed SQLite and chosen DuckDB.
why: The author, 2026-11-12: the whole point of tad is that it can be used with real SQL; and lab-agent's journal will be tad tables that must be queried. The Rust rewrite had dropped SQL as optional - that was wrong.
rejected: No SQL (the rewrite's choice - it left tad unable to answer questions about its own data); GlueSQL (pure Rust, storage as a trait, but younger and a smaller dialect); DataFusion (built for analytics at scale, heavy for this); DuckDB again (a large engine to embed, and the declaration already gives the types).

decision: tad sql runs on DuckDB, as the original research decided: the declared tables are read into DuckDB, the statement runs, and the tables come back through tad's checks and canonical form; whether DuckDB is embedded in tad or called as its pinned standalone binary (as the phone project's feeds already do) is settled by measuring both on the release build.
why: The author, 2026-11-12: SQL was the whole point of tad, researched with prior art before tad existed (why-tad-exists). The 2026-11-12 choice of SQLite contradicted that research, which had weighed SQLite with sqlite-diffable and chosen DuckDB for its native file layout, rich types and measured zero-diff round trip.
rejected: SQLite (weighed in 2026-09, and DuckDB chosen); no SQL (the 2026-11-11 rewrite's mistake).

decision: tad installs its own SQL engine: tad engine fetches DuckDB's pinned binary for this machine into tad's own folder and checks its fingerprint before unpacking; tad sql uses the one named in TAD_DUCKDB, else tad's own, else one on the PATH. The pin lives in the adapter that owns it and moves with tad's releases.
why: An install script copied into each repository is what drifted before (delivering-tad); the DuckDB adapter owns where its engine comes from.
rejected: A copied install-duckdb script in each repository (copies drift); asking each person to install DuckDB themselves (no pin, no fingerprint).

decision: tad's concern is text as data and nothing else: declare the tables, keep them checked and canonical, and make them easy to create, read, update and delete through files, text tools and SQL. Rendering is a use of the data, so it leaves tad for a small tool of its own that consumes tad, taking the presentation declaration ([site], [pages]) out of tables.toml with it; the four repositories' pages are proven byte-identical before tad drops render. tad grows only where working with the data is inconvenient.
why: The author, 2026-11-12: rendering, or any other use of the data, is not tad's concern; it was added in the Python days, before there was anywhere else for it. Half of tad's code (1,288 of 2,601 lines) is rendering; ocoeco uses only tad's check. The renderer becomes its own tool, not part of the observatory's engine, because no project may need the observatory to work: a project draws its own pages.
rejected: Keeping rendering in tad (two concerns in one tool, and presentation mixed into the data's declaration); moving it into the observatory's engine (projects would need the observatory to show their own pages).

decision: When rendering has left, this repository is renamed tad: it then holds only tad. The names tad-engine and text-as-data-template are artifacts of the vendoring era, when the engine was split out to be copied into each repository - an early, hand-made form of what Rhizoid's cuttings are for. text-as-data-template, which still carries the Python engine, is retired with a pointer once nothing starts from it: a new repository starts with ocoeco init and a tables.toml.
why: The author, 2026-11-12: tad and tad-engine come from the old era, explored before rhizoid and rhizcut existed; the template mixed rendering in, and the engine was what tad should be.
rejected: Keeping both names (they describe how tad used to be copied, not what it is); renaming before rendering leaves (the repository would still hold two concerns).
